character.centerRule: Call a figure Satan only when the source names him or links the title in that scene. Keep the serpent in Genesis, Babylon’s king, Tyre’s rulers, Belial, demons, beasts, and unnamed rulers distinct. Join them only when another source makes the link.

phases.orientation: Chronicles, Job, Zechariah, and Wisdom name Satan or the devil. Each source gives him a different setting, limit, action, or result.
phases.title: The adversary is named

phases.orientation: Readers often connect Genesis, Isaiah, and Ezekiel with Satan. Begin with the people and figures each source actually names.
phases.title: Serpent, royal taunts, and contested origins

phases.orientation: The Gospels show the devil testing Jesus through hunger, Scripture, worship, and kingdoms. They tell the tests in different orders.
phases.title: The tempter meets Jesus

phases.orientation: Jesus speaks about Satan through disputed healings, stolen seed, bondage, falling, and rebuke. Human opponents remain responsible for their own actions.
phases.title: Kingdom, word, bondage, and defeat

phases.orientation: The Gospels place Judas, Peter, lies, testing, and the ruler of this world in distinct scenes near Jesus’ death.
phases.title: Betrayal, sifting, and the Passion

phases.orientation: Acts and the letters name Satan or the devil. They show deceit, church discipline, weakness, opposition, and pressure on groups.
phases.title: Schemes, snares, and communities

phases.orientation: Later writings call readers to resist and remain watchful. They also describe the devil’s works, the power of death, and the Lord’s rebuke.
phases.title: Resist, overcome, and destroy

phases.orientation: Revelation names the dragon as the old serpent, devil, and Satan. It follows his accusation, power, deception, limits, and judgment.
phases.title: The dragon is named and judged

character.throughline: Satan appears as an adversary and accuser. He tests and opposes within set limits. The sources show people resisting him and his final defeat. Revelation also calls him the dragon, old serpent, deceiver, accuser, and devil.

edges.basis: Read Job 1:6–12 with Zechariah 3:1–7. Both place Satan before the LORD. Job allows a test. Zechariah gives a rebuke and restores Joshua.

edges.basis: Read Zechariah 3:1–7 with Jude 1:5–10. Both use words of rebuke. The scenes have different speakers and disputed persons.
edges.label: “The LORD rebuke you” in Zechariah and Jude

edges.basis: Read Genesis 3:1–15 with Revelation 12:1–17. Revelation gives the dragon a group of names. Genesis keeps the serpent’s speech and judgment. It does not use the name Satan.

edges.basis: Wisdom 2:21–24 ↔ John 8:39–47: The sources connect the devil with death through different language, audience, and argument.
edges.label: Death, envy, and murder from the beginning

edges.basis: Read Isaiah 14:3–23 with Revelation 12:1–17. Both use images of ascent and fall. They name different figures and use different kinds of writing.
edges.label: A fallen morning star and Satan falling from heaven

edges.basis: Read Ezekiel 28:11–19 with Revelation 12:1–17. Both use high images and expulsion. Only Revelation names Satan.
edges.label: Eden imagery in the Tyre lament and Revelation’s dragon

edges.basis: Matthew 4:1–11 ↔ Luke 4:1–13: Matthew and Luke preserve the same major tests in a different order and close them differently.
edges.label: The order of the wilderness tests

edges.basis: Read Mark 1:9–13 with Matthew 4:1–11. The scenes overlap. Mark is brief. Matthew gives more dialogue and detail.
edges.label: Mark’s brief wilderness scene beside Matthew’s full exchange

edges.basis: Read Matthew 12:22–32 with Luke 11:14–23. Both disputes name Satan’s divided kingdom. Their wording and nearby sayings differ.
edges.label: The divided satanic kingdom in Matthew and Luke

edges.basis: Read Matthew 13:1–23 with Mark 4:1–20. Both explain the seed. They use different names for the hostile actor and stress different parts of hearing.
edges.label: Satan, the devil, and the evil one take the word

edges.basis: Matthew 16:21–28 ↔ Mark 8:27–38: Both witnesses use the same address without saying that Peter has become Satan.
edges.label: “Get behind me, Satan” in Matthew and Mark

edges.basis: Luke 10:17–20 ↔ Revelation 12:7–12: The two falling scenes differ in genre, agents, and narrated consequence.
edges.label: Satan falling in Luke and Revelation

edges.basis: Luke 22:1–6 ↔ John 13:1–30: Luke and John place entry language at different points in their betrayal sequences.
edges.label: When Satan enters Judas

edges.basis: Read Job 1:6–12 with Luke 22:24–34. Both reveal a test hidden from the person tested. They describe the limit and protection in different ways.
edges.label: Permission to test Job and sift the disciples

edges.basis: Read John 13:1–30 with Acts 5:1–11. Both name Satan near a human act. Both still show human intent and responsibility.
edges.label: Satan and human choice in Judas and Ananias

edges.basis: Read 1 Corinthians 5:1–5 with 1 Timothy 1:18–20. Both use the phrase “delivered to Satan.” Each states a different aim in a different church setting.
edges.label: Two people delivered to Satan

edges.basis: Read 2 Corinthians 11:1–15 with Revelation 12:1–17. One source shows a false good appearance and human servants. The other gives open names and angels.
edges.label: An angel-of-light disguise and an openly named dragon

edges.basis: Read 2 Corinthians 12:1–10 with Job 2:1–10. Both name Satan near bodily pain. They differ in cause, prayer, limit, and response.
edges.label: A messenger of Satan and Job’s bodily affliction

edges.basis: Read Ephesians 6:10–20 with 1 Peter 5:6–11. Both call for resistance. They use different images and acts shared by the church.
edges.label: Standing firm against schemes and a prowling foe

edges.basis: 1 John 3:4–12 ↔ Hebrews 2:14–18: The sources describe destruction through different arguments about sin, death, fear, kinship, and help.
edges.label: The Son destroys the devil’s works and power of death

edges.basis: Read Jude 1:5–10 with Revelation 12:1–17. Michael appears in two kinds of writing. He acts differently in each.
edges.label: Michael’s restraint in Jude and conflict in Revelation

edges.basis: Read Revelation 12:1–17 with Revelation 20:1–10. The dragon meets more than one limit. His final judgment comes later. This is not one single fall.
edges.label: The dragon cast down and later bound

edges.basis: Read 2 Thessalonians 2:1–12 with Revelation 13:1–10. The lawless one comes according to Satan’s working. The dragon gives power, a throne, and authority to the beast. The passages do not call every figure Satan.
edges.label: Satanic signs in a letter and Revelation’s beast

edges.basis: Read Matthew 5:33–37 with John 8:39–47. Both link the hostile figure with speech. They address different hearers and acts.
edges.label: Speech from the evil one and the father of lies

edges.basis: Matthew 6:5–15 ↔ John 17:6–19: One source teaches a recurring petition; the other narrates Jesus praying for those he sends.
edges.label: Deliverance from the evil one and Jesus’ prayer for keeping

edges.basis: Read Matthew 25:31–46 with Revelation 20:1–10. Both name a judgment by fire. Only Revelation tells of the devil’s binding, release, and final place.
edges.label: Fire prepared for the devil and the lake-of-fire ending
